Nonetheless, it is evident that expansion of the populationmileage formula will make available to exempt carriers a larger number
of shippers to serve. As the market becomes more attractive in terms
of the volume of traffic available, competition by exempt carriers for
the new traffic may increase; thus increasing the number of carriers
operating in the exempt area. It is asserted that empty mileage and
smaller load factors would be an inevitable result of this increased
competition, thus creating increased fuel consumption, air pollution, and traffic congestion.
Inefficient operations should only occur in the short-run, however. Once the initial competitive period is terminated, only the more efficient operators should survive. The competitive forces, which have historically acted to limit the number of exempt carriers in existing zones, should likewise dictate the number of carriers required to handle the increased traffic in the expanded zones.
The adverse effects identified above should be offset to a certain degree by the beneficial impacts which will accrue to long-haul carriers presented with the opportunity to decrease interline practices.
IV. Alternatives to the Proposed Action
1. No action  One alternative is to retain the present population-mileage formula, and continue to define individual zones when requested to do so. Maintenance of the status quo would foreclose the possibility of additional fuel savings and decreases in air pollution and traffic congestion which is anticipated to result from the contemplated expansion.
2. Eliminate the population-mileage formula completely  A city-by-city commercial zone definition would result in the most accurate reflection of demographic, economic, and industrial characteristics for each city. Many of the representations filed indicate a variety of factual circumstances for various cities, thus leading to the conclusion that individually defined commercial zones would provide the most appropriate method of delineation.
